messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am working with multi-year occupancy data, collected with camera traps and using unmarked::colext() for analysis.

Each detection interval is 14 days. Because cameras sometimes fail, I decided that a camera had to operate for 7 of the 14 days to be included. Otherwise, I replace the value for that camera/interval with an NA.

A coauthor is asking if I can use an offset for this... i.e. using how many days the camera operated in that detection interval as either an offset or covariate on detection.

I know you can use "offsets" in other unmarked models, but not sure if that is available for colext (last thread was like 2015 and it looked not doable at that time). I wonder if a.) offsets work with this model/situation, or if it would be appropriate to use as a detection covariate?

Thanks!

Sarah

messages.body_plain:
Dear Sarah,

I would use the log of the number of days with surveys as a detection covariate. The “real” relationship between detection during the occasion on n days and individual-day detection is given by P = 1 – (1-p)^n. Regressing P on log(n) does a pretty good job at approximating this. See this code:

days <- 1:14

p1 <- 0.2

Ptotal <- 1 - (1-p1)^days

plot(days, Ptotal)

lm(Ptotal ~log(days)) -> fm

pred <- predict(fm)

plot(days, Ptotal)

lines(days, pred)

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Sarah,

I note that how well such a log-linear regression approximates the true relationship depends on the value of the per-day detection probability (p1) as well as on the day range. My values just happened to yield a pretty good approximation, but when you extend the day range to, say, 50, or make p1 smaller or larger, then the approximation will be much less good.

In JAGS it would be easy to specify the model for the exact solution (i.e., using the '1-(1-p)^n' for detection), but in unmarked I don't think you can do this without really going into entrails of the function.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject_clean: Is the hessian available when fitting random effects in occu?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jim,

For a model 'fm' without random effects fit in TMB (with engine="TMB") you can get the hessian like this:

fm@TMB$he()

However TMB does not yet support this for models with random effects (you will get an error). Depending on what you are trying to do, it may be useful to get the joint precision matrix of fixed and random parameters using the TMB::sdreport() function:

jp <- TMB::sdreport(fm@TMB, getJointPrecision=TRUE)

see the docs for TMB::sdreport for more details on this and other stuff it can calculate from the TMB model object. I've been working on easier ways to get this info from unmarked e.g. via the vcov method.

Ken

messages.subject: Nmix.gof.test times out while testing for c-hat for pcount models
messages.subject_clean: Nmix.gof.test times out while testing for c-hat for pcount models
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have successfully calculated c-hat variance inflation factors for several of my unmarked pcount models using Nmix.gof.test in AICcmodavg. Unfortunately, for a subset of models (all of which converged when run), the Nmix.gof.test function continues to run and doesn't stop. I've tried several nsim values from n = 1000 down to nsim = 100. I've even run the gof tests with nsim = 1000 and nsim = 100 for several of the models on an HPC for a week, and they still timed out.

Here is example code:

(more complex model)

m1 <- pcount(~year + time_start + I(time_start^2) + wind ~ veg + I(veg^2) + fruit + I(fruit^2) + water + I(water^2) + drainage + I(drainage^2) + pools + I(pools^2) + dist_des + I(dist_des^2), mixture = 'NB', data = umf.stacked)

m1.gof <- Nmix.gof.test(m1, nsim = 100)

(simpler model)

m2 <- pcount(~year + dayofyear ~ neighborhood_affluence, mixture = 'NB', data = umf.stacked.2)
m2.gof <- Nmix.gof.test(m2, nsim = 100)

My question is, what is the next analytical step? Should I set a fairly arbitrary or conservative c-hat (c-hat = 1, c-hat = 4) and assess these models with a grain of salt? Or should I consider these models non-convergent and only use the set of models from which I was able to calculate c-hat?

Thanks all,

Aaron

Dear Alan,

would help to have a cite for the model. Do you mean Nichols et al. (2008) or Miller et al. (2011) ? If the former, then the answer is "no", if the latter then it is "yes" (this is called 'occuFP').

>From what you say though I think it's the former. ----  But I wonder whether you can't just put all of your data into a single detection history for each site ? E.g., if you distinguish 10 occasions for mist-nets and 50 for the ARUs, then each detection history would have 60 occasions. You could then define an obsCov "method" that has value 1 for the first 10 occasions and value 2 for the remainder (or else code this two-group comparison as 0/1). Fitting that "method" covariate into p should give you an estimate of the per-occasion p's for mist nets and ARUs. Note that to make them perhaps as comparable as possible, you'd have to define the occasions in the same way for both, i.e., to have the same duration.

Or am I missing anything here ?

Best regards  --- Marc

2) ~1 ~(all the variables);
3) ~(all the variables) ~1.

Then, deltaAIC for the selection of which model(s) to be considered has to be calculated manually using all the AIC values.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ken,

I am playing around with the new spOccupancy package to fit spatial occupancy models to big data sets and wanted to compare an analysis with unmarked. It's a static occupancy model with 21,000 sites, 14 occasions and mostly NA's and zeroes (it's for a rare species). I fit a model with two continuous obs covs in detection and 34 (!) continuous site covs in occupancy. Surprisingly I get convergence in unmarked in less than 10 minutes (as opposed to 5 hours in spOccupancy).

However, I get this warning:
Warning message:
Using formula(x) is deprecated when x is a character vector of length > 1.
  Consider formula(paste(x, collapse = " ")) instead.

What does that mean ?

Just for curiosity I attach a plot that compares the MLEs produced by unmarked with the posterior means from spOccupancy. They do match for the most part, but we see that MLE is susceptible to problems with boundary estimates (I believe). Providing solutions from spOccupancy for inits in unmarked helps, but does not avoid this entirely.

Thanks and best regards  ---- Marc

messages.subject_clean: occuRN & presence-only data from multiple years
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

Happy New Year!

Due to its life history and current status, the target species is difficult to count, and preliminary surveys have documented presence-only records over multiple years----some consecutive, others not (e.g., 2005, 2008, and 2017-2019). Managers would like information on abundance to help recover the target (endangered) species.

I am wondering if a Royle-Nichols (i.e., occuRN) model could be used in such a case. My understanding is that colonization-extinction dynamics cannot be incorporated in occuRN models in unmarked; however, perhaps it's advisable to stack records from sites on top of one another over time, while also accounting for survey year as a predictor in abundance- and/or detection-level submodels.

For example, a hypothetical data frame:
Location,    Replicate,    Year,    Presence (1) or "Absence" (0),    Temperature,    Effort,
             A,                  1,    2021,                                                     1,                      10,         2.5,
             A,                  2,    2021,                                                     0,                      15,         1.4,
             A,                  3,    2021,                                                     1,                      13,         2.2,
             A,                  1,    2022,                                                     0,                      17,         1.3,
             A,                  2,    2022,                                                     0,                      19,         1.9,
             A,                  3,    2022,                                                     1,                      22,         2.7,
...

Then the site-level dependent variable and covariate UnmarkedFrame:
        y.1,    Temperature,    Year,
A        1,                       10,   2021,
A        0,                       15,   2021,
A        1,                       13,   2021,
A        0,                       17,   2022,
A        0,                       19,   2022,
A        1,                       22,   2022,
...

With observation-level covariate UnmarkedFrame:
Effort
                 Replicate 1,    Replicate 2,    Replicate 3,
2021A                    2.5,                  1.4,                   2.2,
2022A                    1.3,                  1.9,                   2.7,
...

And, lastly, a candidate model:
occuRN(~ Effort + Year ~ Temperature + Year, data=umf, ...)

Would this be appropriate? Any recommendations on how best to proceed? I also suspect that resultant estimates would be biased high due to species status and the model lacking dynamism.

Perhaps a different unmarked model or ensemble of models is better suited for this problem; otherwise, data may need to be modeled one year at a time. I also hope I have represented the hypothetical data appropriately, in particular without formatting errors. Please forgive any mistakes to the contrary.

Thanks,
Andrew
